## How it works

Caddy holds its entire configuration as a single JSON document, which it
serves and accepts over its [admin
API](https://caddyserver.com/docs/api) (`http://localhost:2019` by
default). fastcaddy talks to that API; it never touches a Caddyfile.

There are two layers here:

- **Primitives** map 1:1 to admin API operations:
  [`gcfg`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#gcfg)/[`pcfg`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#pcfg)
  get and set config subtrees by path,
  [`gid`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#gid)/[`pid`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#pid)/[`del_id`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#del_id)
  do the same for objects tagged with an `@id`,
  [`has_path`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#has_path)/[`has_id`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#has_id)
  test for existence, and
  [`reset`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#reset)
  erases everything.
- **Recipes**
  ([`setup_caddy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#setup_caddy),
  [`add_reverse_proxy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_reverse_proxy),
  [`add_wildcard_route`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_wildcard_route),
  [`add_sub_reverse_proxy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_sub_reverse_proxy),
  [`add_on_demand_tls`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_on_demand_tls))
  each own one documented subtree of the config, and are safe to re-run:
  they replace or skip their own subtree and never touch anything else.

Config set over the API is *ephemeral*: it does not survive a caddy
restart unless you arrange that yourself. The recommended pattern (used
by our production apps) is a setup script that runs on every deploy:
[`reset()`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#reset),
then the recipes you need. That way the script is the single source of
truth for your routing config.

Routes created by the recipes are tagged with predictable `@id`s, which
is how re-runs find and replace them: a plain reverse proxy is tagged
with its hostname, a wildcard route for `*.{domain}` is tagged
`wildcard-{domain}`, and a subdomain proxy inside it is tagged
`{subdomain}.{domain}`.
[`del_id`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#del_id)
removes any of them.

``` python
from fastcore.test import *
```

## Admin API primitives

These wrap the admin API endpoints directly. `/config/` addresses config
subtrees by path; `/id/` addresses any config object that carries an
`"@id"` key, no matter where it lives in the tree.

The admin API location comes from the `CADDY_ADMIN` env var if set. To
point somewhere else at runtime, set `fastcaddy.core.admin_url`
directly.

### pcfg

``` python
def pcfg(
    d, path:str='/', method:str='post'
):
```

*Put/post config `d` at `path`*

`method` follows caddy’s semantics: `post` sets a value (appending, when
the target is an array), `put` creates a new value and fails with a 409
if the path already exists (creating any missing parent levels on the
way), `patch` replaces an existing value, and `delete` removes one.

Two things to know about caddy paths: getting a missing key under an
existing object returns `null` rather than an error (only traversing
*through* a missing key fails), which is why
[`has_path`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#has_path)
checks for `None`; and posting to `'/'` replaces the *entire* config –
that’s what
[`reset`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#reset) is
for, and nothing else here does it implicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fastcaddy/blob/main/fastcaddy/core.py#L88"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### reset

``` python
def reset():
```

*Erase the entire caddy config*

On a fresh (or just-reset) caddy, the config is simply empty:

``` python
reset()
gcfg()
```

## TLS automation

Caddy issues certificates according to [automation
policies](https://caddyserver.com/docs/json/apps/tls/automation/) under
`/apps/tls/automation`. Two recipes set up the first policy:
[`add_acme_config`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_acme_config)
for real certificates (ACME with cloudflare DNS challenges – what you
want in production), and
[`add_tls_internal_config`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_tls_internal_config)
for caddy’s internal CA (local development). Both are no-ops if any
automation config already exists, and neither touches anything outside
`/apps/tls/automation`.

``` python
cf_token = os.environ.get('CADDY_CF_TOKEN', 'XXX')
```

To enable\nit, create an automation policy with `on_demand`.\n\n\nOnDemandConfig configures on-demand TLS, for obtaining\nneeded certificates at handshake-time. Because this\nfeature can easily be abused, Caddy must ask permission\nto your application whether a particular domain is allowed\nto have a certificate issued for it.\n"

## Routes and reverse proxies

80 and 443. All routes live in its `routes` list; each recipe below adds

``` python
def setup_caddy(

    local:bool=False, # Use caddy's internal CA instead of ACME (for local dev)
    install_trust:bool=None, # Install the local CA into the system trust store?

):
```

*Create TLS automation config and the http server skeleton*

[`setup_caddy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#setup_caddy)
is the one-call version of the above: TLS automation (ACME by default,
internal CA with `local=True`), optional trust-store installation, and
the `srv0` server skeleton. In production:

``` python

```

For local dev (which is also how the rest of this notebook runs – note
that the earlier
[`reset`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#reset) means
the internal CA policy is created fresh here):

``` python
setup_caddy(local=True)
gcfg(srvs_path)
```

<div class="prose" data-markdown="1">

``` python
{ '@id': 'foo.example.com',
  'handle': [{'encodings': {'gzip': {'level': 1}, 'zstd': {'level': 'fastest'}}, 'handler': 'encode', 'prefer': ['zstd', 'gzip']}, {'handler': 'reverse_proxy', 'stream_close_delay': '1m', 'upstreams': [{'dial': 'localhost:5001'}]}],
  'match': [{'host': ['foo.example.com']}],
  'terminal': True}
```

</div>

Calling it again for the same host *replaces* the route (same `@id`, new
target) rather than adding a duplicate:

``` python
n = len(gcfg(rts_path))
add_reverse_proxy(host, "localhost:8000")
test_eq(len(gcfg(rts_path)), n)
test_eq(gid(host).handle[1].upstreams[0].dial, 'localhost:8000')
```

[`del_id`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#del_id)
removes it – and keeps going until no route with that `@id` remains, so
even ids duplicated via raw
[`add_route`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_route)
are fully cleared:

``` python
add_route({"@id": host, "handle": [proxy_handler('localhost:9999')]})
del_id(host)
test_eq(has_id(host), False)
```

### On-demand TLS

On-demand TLS makes caddy obtain a certificate *at handshake time* for
domains it has never seen – the mechanism behind letting customers point
their own domains at your app. To stop strangers minting certs through
your server, caddy first asks your `endpoint`
(`GET {endpoint}?domain={domain}`) and only proceeds on a 200 response.
`tools/testverify.py` in this repo is a minimal fasthtml example of such
an endpoint.

[`add_on_demand_tls`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_on_demand_tls)
sets the permission endpoint and ensures one automation policy with
`on_demand: true` exists, appending it after any existing policies (it
never replaces them). One caddy rule to know: the on-demand policy is a
*catch-all* (no `subjects`), and caddy rejects a config where a
catch-all follows another catch-all – so any earlier policies must be
subject-restricted, which is why production setups pass `subjects` to
[`setup_caddy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#setup_caddy).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fastcaddy/blob/main/fastcaddy/core.py#L250"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### add_on_demand_tls

``` python
def add_on_demand_tls(
    endpoint
):
```

*Enable on-demand TLS, asking `endpoint` for permission before each cert
is issued*

``` python
setup_caddy(cf_token, subjects=["*.example.com", "example.com"])
add_on_demand_tls("http://localhost:5431/verifydom")
```

Locally we can demonstrate the exact production shape with a
subject-restricted internal policy standing in for the ACME one – the
on-demand policy lands after it, and re-running adds nothing:

``` python
reset()
init_path(automation_path)
pcfg([{'subjects': ['*.example.com'], 'issuers': [{'module': 'internal'}]}], automation_path+'/policies')
add_on_demand_tls("http://localhost:5431/verifydom")
pols = gcfg(automation_path+'/policies')
test_eq(pols[1].on_demand, True)
add_on_demand_tls("http://localhost:5431/verifydom")
test_eq(len(gcfg(automation_path+'/policies')), 2)
```

## Wildcard subdomains

For many subdomains of one domain, a wildcard route is better than
per-host routes: caddy can then use a single wildcard certificate
(`*.{domain}`), and subdomains route through a `subroute` handler inside
it. Create the wildcard once, then add each subdomain with
[`add_sub_reverse_proxy`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_sub_reverse_proxy)
(or a custom route with
[`add_sub_route`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_sub_route)).

[`add_wildcard_route`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_wildcard_route)
is a no-op if the wildcard already exists – replacing it would destroy
the subroutes inside – so re-running a setup script keeps existing
subdomains intact.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fastcaddy/blob/main/fastcaddy/core.py#L266"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### add_wildcard_route

``` python
def add_wildcard_route(
    domain
):
```

*Add a route matching `*.{domain}` (tagged `wildcard-{domain}`) for
subroutes; no-op if it already exists*

``` python
reset()
setup_caddy(local=True)
add_wildcard_route('something.example.com')
add_wildcard_route('something.example.com')
test_eq(sum(1 for o in gcfg(rts_path) if o['@id']=='wildcard-something.example.com'), 1)
```

[`add_sub_route`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#add_sub_route)
is how routes get *inside* the wildcard: it appends to the subroute
list, replacing any existing route with the same `@id`. This is also the
extension point for custom handlers (our production config pushes an
`encode` + custom router + `reverse_proxy` chain through it).

target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>


existing route with the same `@id`*

### add_sub_reverse_proxy

``` python
def add_sub_reverse_proxy(
    domain, # Domain with an existing wildcard route
    subdomain, # Subdomain to proxy (tagged `{subdomain}.{domain}`)
    port:Union, # A single port or list of ports
    host:str='localhost', # Host the upstream(s) listen on
    st_delay:str='1m', # Keep streaming connections open this long across config reloads (None to disable)
    encode:bool=True, # Compress responses?
):
```

*Create (or replace) a reverse proxy to `{subdomain}.{domain}` inside
`domain`’s wildcard route*

``` python
add_sub_reverse_proxy('something.example.com', 'foo', 5001)
gid('foo.something.example.com')
```

<div class="prose" data-markdown="1">

``` python
{ '@id': 'foo.something.example.com',
  'handle': [{'encodings': {'gzip': {'level': 1}, 'zstd': {'level': 'fastest'}}, 'handler': 'encode', 'prefer': ['zstd', 'gzip']}, {'handler': 'reverse_proxy', 'stream_close_delay': '1m', 'upstreams': [{'dial': 'localhost:5001'}]}],
  'match': [{'host': ['foo.something.example.com']}]}
```

</div>

Re-adding the same subdomain replaces its route rather than duplicating
it, multiple ports become multiple upstreams, and
[`del_id`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/fastcaddy/core.html#del_id)
deletes it as usual:

``` python
add_sub_reverse_proxy('something.example.com', 'foo', [5002, 5003])
subs = gid('wildcard-something.example.com').handle[0].routes
test_eq(len(subs), 1)
test_eq([u.dial for u in subs[0].handle[1].upstreams], ['localhost:5002', 'localhost:5003'])
```

``` python
del_id('foo.something.example.com')
test_eq(has_id('foo.something.example.com'), False)
```
